justice: The street provides a very wide paved carriageway with orderly tree belts on both sides, but no visible sidewalk space is clearly defined, suggesting road space is allocated more strongly to motor movement than to pedestrians.

No marked crosswalks, curb ramps, tactile paving, or pedestrian refuge features are visible, which weakens accessibility for a broad range of users even though the corridor appears physically open and unobstructed.

Streetlights are present along the road edges, indicating some public investment distributed along the corridor, but the absence of visible pedestrian-specific facilities makes the environment less equitable for non-drivers.
safety: The road is straight, wide, and has clear centerline markings, which supports predictable vehicle movement and good forward visibility.

Rows of streetlights are visible on both sides, which can improve nighttime traffic safety, although their effectiveness for pedestrians cannot be confirmed because no sidewalk zone is clearly visible.

Safety for walking is limited by the lack of visible crosswalks, traffic calming, protected pedestrian space, or bike lanes, so vulnerable road users would have little dedicated protection if present.
livability: Dense rows of mature trees on both sides create a greener and calmer setting than a fully built-up arterial, improving environmental quality.
The corridor appears almost entirely dedicated to through movement, with no visible shops, benches, bus stops, plazas, or active frontages that would support everyday social life.
The scene feels quiet and low-density, but the absence of visible destinations or public-use amenities reduces its usefulness as a lively, multi-purpose street environment.
sustainability: Extensive tree cover along both sides contributes to shade, carbon uptake, and a greener roadside landscape.
There are no visible bike lanes, bus stops, or other clear low-carbon transport facilities, so sustainable mobility support appears limited in the image.

The landscaped edges with trees and planted ground surfaces are more ecologically beneficial than fully paved shoulders, though no visible stormwater features or permeable pedestrian areas can be confirmed.
aesthetics: The long symmetrical perspective of the straight road, repeated streetlights, and aligned utility poles creates strong visual order.
Large, healthy-looking trees on both sides frame the corridor and soften the otherwise hard asphalt surface.
The roadway appears clean, well maintained, and uncluttered, which enhances visual neatness despite the dominance of utility infrastructure overhead.
comfort: Tree canopies provide intermittent shade along the edges, but the center of the wide asphalt roadway is fully exposed to sun, limiting thermal comfort for users outside the shaded margins.
The pavement surface looks smooth and even for vehicle travel, which supports physical comfort for drivers, but no benches, shelters, or pedestrian resting facilities are visible.
The corridor appears uncrowded and visually open, which can support psychological comfort, yet the lack of dedicated pedestrian space may make non-motorized users feel less at ease.
walkability: No clearly visible sidewalks or separated pedestrian paths can be identified, making walking infrastructure weak from an all-road-users perspective.
There are no visible crosswalks, curb ramps, pedestrian signals, or refuge islands, so crossing opportunities and route connectivity for walkers appear poor.
Although the corridor is lined with trees and looks orderly, the street functions mainly as a movement corridor rather than a pedestrian-oriented place, which lowers overall walkability.
